analysis.one_liner: Bans health insurers and employers from discriminating based on genetic test results or family medical history.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by the Senate's top Democrat and cosponsored by 29 of 49 Senate Democrats, got two committee hearings but never a committee vote or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for health insurers to deny coverage, raise premiums, or require genetic testing based on a person's genetic information, including family disease history. It would also make it illegal for employers, job agencies, unions, and training programs to hire, fire, or classify workers based on genetic information, or to demand genetic tests from workers or applicants. It covered group and individual insurance, Medicare supplement policies, and employment, and let people sue or complain to the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission when violated.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who has taken a genetic test or could in the future, and their families. It would let people learn their genetic risks through testing without fear of losing their health insurance or their job, since insurers could not use test results or family history to deny enrollment or set rates, and employers could not use that information in hiring, firing, or workplace training decisions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who take genetic tests and their families

how_it_helps.text: Insurers could not deny or condition enrollment, adjust premiums, request or require genetic tests, or collect or buy genetic information in group plans, individual plans, or Medicare supplement policies, except for limited claims-payment purposes or with the person's written authorization [S2][S3].

Employers, employment agencies, labor organizations, and apprenticeship programs could not discriminate against anyone because of protected genetic information, and could not request, require, collect, or purchase genetic tests or information except in narrow cases such as workplace-toxin monitoring or voluntary, employee-authorized services [S2][S3].

The bill let individuals and labor organizations sue in federal or state court, allowed attorney's fees and expert costs, and gave the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission enforcement powers; states could keep stronger protections of their own [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers would bear the cost of compliance and of losing the ability to screen people out or price coverage based on genetic risk. If people with genetic risks could no longer be priced separately, some of that cost would be spread across all premium payers in a risk pool.

drawbacks.text: Barring insurers from using genetic information can raise premiums for everyone: people who learn they carry disease risk would have a stronger incentive to buy coverage while healthy people might buy less, leaving insurers with a costlier pool whose costs are shared by all enrollees rather than priced to individual risk [S3].

The bill deliberately left current health status, age, and sex outside its definition of protected genetic information, so insurers and employers could still discriminate based on existing diagnosed conditions; the bill protected genetic risk but not all health-based discrimination [S3].

Employers would lose flexibility in medical screening of applicants and employees, facing lawsuits for practices they previously used, though the bill preserved limited screening tied to diagnosing a current condition that would prevent someone from doing the job [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people weighing a genetic test, the benefit is substantial and direct: the freedom to learn about inherited disease risk without putting insurance or employment at stake. The costs are real but diffuse: somewhat higher premiums spread across insurance pools and litigation risk for employers. The bill's own carve-outs for claims payment, workplace monitoring, and current health status narrowed its economic impact on insurers compared with the fears its title might suggest.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate health committee held two hearings on the bill but never voted to send it to the full Senate, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Daschle introduced the bill on February 13, 2001, joined by 16 other Senate Democrats as original cosponsors [S3][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, which was its only committee referral [S5].
The committee held hearings on July 25, 2001 and again on February 13, 2002, printing them as S.Hrg. 107-178 and S.Hrg. 107-286 [S5].
The bill never received a committee vote, was never reported to the Senate floor, and never received any vote in either chamber before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].
All 29 cosponsors were Democrats, 29 of the Senate's 49 Democrats; no Republican cosponsored [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers that would have been restricted came out ahead, since they kept the ability to use genetic information in underwriting and personnel decisions. Americans weighing genetic testing also lost the protection and, without it, had reason to avoid tests they might have taken.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers kept the status quo

for.name: Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 16 Senate Democrats as original cosponsors

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Held hearings in July 2001 and February 2002 but never voted to report the bill to the Senate

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Senate Democrat (29 of 49, including the Democratic leader), with no Republican cosponsor, and the bill never reached a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would strip insurers of the ability to deny enrollment, raise premiums, or require genetic tests based on genetic information in group, individual, and Medicare supplement markets. Insurers priced by genetic risk to keep high-risk people out; blocking that shifts sick-risk protection to ordinary policyholders.

The bill would bar employers from requesting genetic tests or using genetic information in hiring, firing, and training, with narrow exceptions for workplace-toxin monitoring and voluntary, employee-authorized services. Employers could no longer screen workers or applicants for genetic risk, and would face lawsuits under the bill's enforcement provisions.

industries.industry: Medical Information Bureau and insurance data clearinghouses
industries.note: The bill would prohibit insurers from disclosing genetic information to the Medical Information Bureau or any similar collector of insurance information, cutting off a channel that would otherwise make genetic data available industry-wide.
By removing the insurance and job consequences of testing, the bill would give people a reason to undergo genetic services they might otherwise avoid, expanding the market for testing and counseling.
